newsitem.title: HUNGARY: MOL'S RECORD GAS DEAL NOT ALL GOOD NEWS - ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: MOL'S RECORD GAS DEAL NOT ALL GOOD NEWS - ANALYSTS.

text.p: A massive deal for Russia's Panrusgaz to supply Hungarian oil and gas company Magyar Olaj- es Gazipari Rt will not be all good news for MOL, analysts said on Monday.
"While assuming that the price is decent... I have mixed feelings about this contract," Frances Cloud of Nomura Securities in London told Reuters.
MOL and Panrusgaz said on Friday they had signed a contract for the delivery of 225 billion cubic meters of Russian natural gas to Hungary over 20 years.
The two companies did not give prices of the deal, only said that the terms of the contract are in line with Western European standards.
"This contract could mean that MOL is not expecting to get gas from anywhere else," Cloud said.
Gas wholesale in Hungary is a MOL monopoly, but Panrusgaz officials have said they also plan to enter the market, and this possibility also raises some questions, Cloud said.
"Will MOL then be still forced to pay for this gas even though they can't sell it themselves?" Cloud asked.
The picture is somewhat blurred by the fact that Panrusgaz is a joint venture half owned by MOL and half by Russia's RAO Gazprom, Gabor Sitanyi, ING Barings' London-based analyst, said.
"It is an absurd situation when a company signs such a contract with its own subsidiary," he added.

On the other hand, MOL, with its 50 percent stake in Panrusgaz, will also have a say in the decision to apply for a gas wholesale licence, Sitanyi said, adding that Hungary is not Gazprom's prime target.

"Gazprom's main target are the western European countries," he said. "There could be some additional profit in selling gas to Hungary beside of transiting it, but I don't think this is a major issue for Gazprom."
He was not overly cencerned about MOL not being able to sell the gas already contracted.
"MOL itself could have plans for wholesale in other countries," Sitanyi said. "On the whole, positive aspects of the contract weigh heavier in the balance."

Although current estimates forecast Hungary's gas consumption to grow to around 15 billion cubic meters per year by 2010, from the current 11 billion cubic meters, this might be a questionable figure.
"It could largely depend on how many gas-fired power stations will be built over the next years," Sitanyi said.
He also said MOL's dependence on Gazprom due to this deal is something the company can do little about.
"Sooner or later everybody will depend on Russian gas," Sitanyi said. "If the whole of Europe stopped extracting gas, Russia could still supply the continent for at least another one hundred years."
